item: Securities industry employment, New York City (NAICS 523, OSC/NYS DOL basis)
then_value: 201,100 jobs in 2000 (record); 2001 level not stated, but 32,800 securities jobs lost in 2001
then_quote: In the securities sector, job losses slowed from 32,800 in 2001 to 2,300 in 2002.  Nonetheless, since employment in this sector peaked at the end of 2000 (one month before the peak for the overall City economy), job losses ha ve totaled 35,300 —a 17.6 percent decline.
now_quote: employment edged down slightly to 198,200 in 2025 from a 30-year high of 201,500 in 2024
notes: 2000 record from OSC Report 15-2026 (Oct 2025, https://www.osc.ny.gov/files/reports/pdf/report-15-2026.pdf): 'In 2024, the Current Employment Statistics (CES) data showed employment at securities firms in the City increased by 3,100 jobs (1.6 percent) to a total of 201,500 jobs, eclipsing the record high of 201,100 in 2000 (see Figure 8).' No document fetched states a 2001 annual level for NAICS 523; the OSC April 2003 report is SIC-based. QCEW 2024 annual avg for NAICS 523 private, five counties summed from https://data.bls.gov/cew/data/api/2024/a/industry/523.csv = 193,376 (Manhattan 191,173); QCEW API returns 404 for 2001. Narrower consistent series, NYS DOL CES line 55523100 'Securities and Commodity Contracts Intermediation and Brokerage' (NAICS 5231) for New York City from ces.csv: Aug 2001 145,900 / 2001 annual 141,000 vs Jul 2026 110,000 / 2025 annual 104,600 — brokerage headcount is DOWN about a quarter since 2001 while the broader 523 (which adds fund/portfolio management and investment advice) is roughly flat with 2000. Use the DOL pair only with that scope caveat.

item: Securities industry share of New York City wages
then_value: 21.3% of total wages paid in NYC (5.2% of the labor force)
then_quote: Overall, Wall Street accounted for 21.3 percent of total wages paid in New York City in 2001 (but employ ed only 5.2 percent of the City’s labor force).
now_value: 20% of private-sector wages (4.8% of private-sector employment)
now_quote: The industry accounted for more than half (59 percent) of all private sector bonus payments and 20 percent of private sector wages in New York City in 2024, while accounting for a relatively small share (4.8 percent) of private sector employment.
notes: Denominators differ: 2001 figure is share of TOTAL wages (SIC-era definition), 2024 is share of PRIVATE-SECTOR wages. City tax share now: 'The industry accounted for an estimated 8.4 percent of City tax collections in CFY 2025, an increase from the prior year’s share of 6.7 percent and above pre-pandemic levels.' (same Oct 2025 report). No fetched 2001 tax-share figure.

NBC News (Sept. 16, 2003, news fallback) also says: 'The total number of visitors who came to New York City was up 0.3 percent from 2001, when the Sept. 11 air attacks made many global and domestic tourists fear flying.' — implying ~35.2M for 2001. The 2000 record is primary: Mayor's press release #264-01, July 30, 2001, https://www.nyc.gov/html/om/html/2001b/pr264-01.html: 'the City welcomed a record 37.4 million visitors in 2000'. 2025 release (March 24, 2026) also: 'Overall visitation generated $84.7 billion in total economic impact, including $55.6 billion in direct spending' and 'The tourism sector accounts for 397,000 jobs'. 2019 record was 66.6M.

item: Rental vacancy rate, New York City Housing and Vacancy Survey
then_quote: The 2002 HVS reports a citywide rental vacancy rate of 2.94 percent during the period between February and June of 2002.
now_quote: New York City's vacancy rate has dropped to a mere 1.4 percent – the lowest this measurement has been since the 1968 NYCHVS.
notes: HPD, 'Selected Findings of the 2002 New York City Housing and Vacancy Survey'. 2023 HVS is the latest released; HPD release also: 'In a mere two years, the vacancy rate nosedived from 4.54%, illuminating a profound scarcity of available homes for rent.'
